name: Yara Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on night response in the Riverside Quarter, which is all bars, kebab shops and two big clubs. A shift runs eight at night to six in the morning, four on, four off. Most calls are fights, people who've lost their friends, and a lot of mental health crises that land on us because nobody else is open at 3am. I like being the calm one in a messy room.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned mental health calls. How much of your night is that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On a Friday, maybe a third. Last year I did a six-month pilot where a mental health nurse rode with me, and it was the best work I've ever done. The pilot ended when the money ran out. I've been trying to get back into something like it ever since.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, now can we talk about what actually needs fixing, which is mental health cover at night. I'd probably post something about that, because it gets lost every time tech is in the news. At work I'd just shrug, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means not much changes for me, and that's alright. I'd still be dealing with the same Friday-night chaos and the same paperwork. The transcription tool I use now and then for body-cam notes would get a bit better, and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing nights and keep pushing my inspector to bring back the nurse pilot. I'd keep putting money into the index fund my aunt helped me start when I was nineteen. Tomas (my partner) and I would carry on saving for a house deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'm well paid for my level, we've got about nine months put by, and there are always jobs for police officers. My stress comes from the shifts, not from the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your stress comes from the shifts. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sleeping till two in the afternoon and seeing my partner for an hour is the thing that would make me leave nights, not AI. Tomas is a history teacher, so our clocks are completely opposite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push for anything politically in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, for proper funding of a night mental health service. I'd write to the police and crime office about the pilot, because it saved hours of officer time. I'd rather the AI money went there.

say: Fine, now let's fix **mental health cover** at night instead.
The tech hype always **buries** the real problems on our streets.
think: Not much changes for me, and **that's alright**.
My body-cam **transcription tool** gets a bit better, and that's it.
do: **Keep working** nights in the Riverside Quarter and push for the **nurse pilot**.
**Keep paying** into the index fund and the house deposit with Tomas.
**Write** to the police and crime office about night mental health funding.
feel: **Calm**, because her pay, savings and job options are solid.
**Tired** from opposite body clocks with Tomas, not from AI.
S0.quote: Sleeping till two in the afternoon and seeing my partner for an hour is the thing that would make me leave nights, not AI.
fieldNote: Her real pressure is **night shifts** and time with Tomas, not technology.
She steers every question back to **mental health** cover, her passion.
Already uses a **transcription tool** now and then, without fuss.

steps.text: Keep working night response in the Riverside Quarter
Keep saving for a house deposit with Tomas
Write to the police and crime office about the nurse pilot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI writing our reports is fine as long as the time saved goes back into people, not cuts. I'd back the union's line that no posts disappear. Online I'd probably share stuff about AI being used to triage mental health calls, because that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it changes my nights a lot. The call handling and the reports are thinking work, and that's probably 40 percent of my shift. I could see them saying one van can cover what two used to, and I'd be on my own more at 3am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the report software properly once a couple of colleagues swear by it, not before. I'd start looking at a part-time social work course, because that's where I see a future that machines can't touch. And I'd get more active in the union, maybe go to meetings instead of just reading the emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't think I lose my job, but the job around me gets thinner and lonelier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be on your own more at 3am. What does that mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means waiting longer for backup when a fight spills out of the club on Ferry Street. Last month I waited eleven minutes with a man bleeding on the pavement. Eleven minutes alone is a long time in a crowd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why social work rather than something with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A machine is the last thing a person in crisis wants to talk to, and sitting on the kerb with them is the bit I'm good at. I'd rather get better at that than at managing software.

say: AI reports are fine if the **time saved** goes back into **people**, not cuts.
Using AI to **triage** mental health calls should scare everyone.
think: About **40 percent** of my shift is thinking work that AI could take.
I could end up **alone more** at 3am if one van covers two.
do: **Learn** the report software once a few colleagues swear by it.
**Go to** union meetings instead of just reading the emails.
feel: **Uneasy**, seeing the job around her get **thinner** and lonelier.
S1.quote: A machine is the last thing a person in crisis wants to talk to, and sitting on the kerb with them is the bit I'm good at.
fieldNote: Her worry is **safety and backup**, not her pay; the eleven-minute wait sticks with her.
She'd **learn AI** only after others prove it, true to her steady nature.
Social work is her **planned escape**, chosen for meaning, not fear.

steps.text: Learn the new report software once colleagues rate it
Apply for a part-time social work course
Start going to union branch meetings in person

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need officers more than ever when everything is changing that fast, because people get scared and angry. I'd be at the union meetings and at any protest about cuts. Online I'd post that nobody voted for robot police.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think by 2028 the control room and all our paperwork is AI, and by 2031 a robot could probably handle a fight outside a club better than a five-foot-four woman. The bit I'd still do is the human stuff, the crisis calls. But I don't know if anyone would pay for that once the rest is automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the social work degree part-time straight away, not in a year. Tomas and I would put the house deposit on hold, because I don't want a mortgage on a job that might not be there in 2031. And I'd keep the nine months of savings untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because we've got money and two incomes, but my own job feels like it has an end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before the robots give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to finish most of a degree while still being paid as an officer. Thinking AI would hit the paperwork first, so I'd be on the streets even more for those three years. I'd use every quiet shift to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas the night you decided to pause the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomas that I'd rather rent for three more years than lie awake about a mortgage on a police job that might not be there in 2031. He'd agree, he's more careful than me. His job feels safer than mine in that world, and that's a strange thing to admit.

say: People need **officers** most when everything changes fast.
**Nobody voted** for robot police, and I'd say so at protests.
think: By **2028** the control room and paperwork are AI; by **2031** robots handle fights.
Nobody may **pay for** the human crisis work once the rest is automated.
do: **Start** the social work degree part-time **straight away**.
**Pause** the house deposit plan with Tomas until after 2031.
**Keep** the nine months of savings untouched.
feel: **Anxious**, as if her own job now has an **end date**.
Steadied by **two incomes** and savings, so not panicked.
S2.quote: I'd rather rent for three more years than lie awake about a mortgage on a police job that might not be there in 2031.
fieldNote: She sees **physical policing** as the part robots do better than her, an honest admission.
Pausing the **house** is the clearest sign this picture worries her.
The **three-year gap** becomes study time, not breathing room.

steps.text: Enrol part-time on a social work degree this year
Pause the house deposit plan with Tomas until 2031
Keep nine months of savings untouched as a buffer
Join union protests against cuts to officer numbers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something better, like a proper night crisis service with officers in it. I'd push that line at work and online. I'd be less angry than in the fast one, more organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's still the end of the job as I know it, just slower. Paperwork goes by 2031 and robots by 2034, when I'd be 35. That's enough time to switch to social work without a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the social work degree next September, part-time, and finish it while still on nights. I'd use the AI tools more, since by then everyone would, and they'd save me time for study. Tomas and I would probably still buy the house, just a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a plan, and having a plan makes it feel like my choice instead of something done to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still buy a house. Isn't that a risk if the job goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but Tomas's teaching pay would cover a small place on its own. And with five years' notice I'd be qualified in something else before the robots arrive. That's the difference from the fast picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older sergeants who've done nothing but this for twenty years. My sergeant Wendy is 52 and says she'll go before she learns another system. Five years isn't much for her.

say: Five years is enough to build a **night crisis service** with officers in it.
I'd be **more organised** and less angry than in the fast picture.
think: It's still the **end of the job** as I know it, just slower.
Robots by **2034** leave time to switch to **social work** calmly.
do: **Start** a part-time social work degree next **September**.
**Use** AI tools more to free up time for study.
**Buy** a smaller house with Tomas, covered by his pay.
feel: **Uneasy**, but a plan makes it feel like **her choice**.
S3.quote: Having a plan makes it feel like my choice instead of something done to me.
fieldNote: The extra years change her from **defensive** to **organised**.
Tomas's **teaching pay** is her quiet safety net for the house.
She worries about older colleagues like **Wendy**, more than herself.

steps.text: Start a part-time social work degree next September
Use the force's AI report tools to free up study time
Buy a smaller house with Tomas that his pay covers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's design policing around people for once. I'd want the force to build the night crisis team now, not wait. I'd be pretty upbeat about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm fine in this one. Ten years means I'd be 37 when the thinking AI is everywhere and 40 when the robots come. I'd have moved into crisis work long before then, maybe even led a team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the social work degree over four years without rushing, and apply for any crisis team role that comes up. I'd learn the AI tools as they become normal at the station. Tomas and I would buy the house and maybe think about kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Ten years is a whole career for some people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different about kids in this picture compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the fast one, I wouldn't bring a baby into that year. With ten years I can see the ground under my feet. I'd still be careful, but I wouldn't be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this slower version that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people will waste the ten years. The force let my nurse pilot lapse in six months, and I worry they'll waste ten years of warning the same way.

say: Ten years is plenty, so **design policing** around people for once.
The force should build the **night crisis team** now.
think: I'm **fine** here: 37 when AI spreads and **40** when robots come.
I'd have moved into **crisis work** long before, maybe leading a team.
do: **Study** social work over **four years** without rushing.
**Apply** for crisis team roles as they open.
**Buy** the house with Tomas and start thinking about **kids**.
feel: **Calm**, because ten years is a whole career.
Slightly **wary** that the force will waste the warning time.
S4.quote: The force let my nurse pilot lapse in six months, and I worry they'll waste ten years of warning the same way.
fieldNote: Ten years turns this into a **career opportunity** for her.
**Kids** become possible only in the slow picture, a clear marker of security.
Her doubt is about **institutions**, not her own ability to adapt.

steps.text: Study social work part-time over four years
Apply for night crisis team roles as they open
Buy the house with Tomas and plan for children
Learn the station's AI tools as they become normal

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, the fast one, because the robots would arrive just as I'd finished retraining, with nothing in between. What would help is the force paying for officers to retrain into crisis and social work while still on full pay. That, and a guarantee that a human answers every mental health call.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how this lands for women in the job. A lot of the physical side is where people doubt us anyway. If robots take the physical side of policing, maybe women officers are the ones who stay, doing the talking. I'd like to think that, anyway.

headlineQuote: If robots take the physical side of policing, maybe women officers are the ones who stay, doing the talking.
portrait: Yara is a **27-year-old** night response officer in the Riverside Quarter's bars and clubs.
She has **nine months saved**, an index fund and a partner, Tomas, who teaches history.
Her passion is **mental health** crisis work since a six-month nurse pilot ended.
She adopts AI tools **once proven** and plans a move into **social work**.
Her mood tracks **warning time**: calm with ten years, anxious with two.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive just as she finishes **retraining**.
whatWouldHelp: Force-paid **retraining** into crisis and social work on full pay.
A guarantee that a **human answers** every mental health call.
